In *Early-Token Confidence Predicts Reasoning Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate* [[1]](#ref-1), Keramati et al. (UC Irvine) show that the confidence of an LLM's first few generated tokens predicts how a judge rates the quality of its reasoning in a debate-based essay-scoring system, often better than statistics taken over the whole response.

> Evaluating reasoning quality in multi-agent LLM systems is challenging, especially for open-ended tasks without reference answers. We investigate whether *intrinsic confidence signals, token-level log-probabilities from decoding, can predict reasoning quality as assessed by LLM-as-judge evaluation*. Using a debate-based essay scoring framework, we compare confidence proxies against rubric-based judge scores across two ASAP essay sets. We find that *early-token confidence, particularly within the first few generated tokens, is consistently the strongest predictor of reasoning quality*, outperforming full-sequence statistics. Analysis of log-probability trajectories shows that *the opening phase of generation is the most heterogeneous and therefore most informative*. We also observe *a systematic asymmetry between agent roles, with stronger alignment between confidence and quality for supportive reasoning than for adversarial critique*. These results suggest that *early decoding dynamics provide a lightweight and effective signal for estimating reasoning reliability* in multi-agent LLM systems.

## Methods

The framework scores essays through a structured debate, then mines the debaters' own decoding signals rather than any reference answer:

- **Two debating agents**: an Advocate argues an essay's strengths against a rubric trait and a Skeptic rebuts with limitations, both producing open-ended argument without assigning a score. Both are generated by GPT-4o-mini.
- **Confidence signals**: during decoding, each agent's per-token log-probabilities $\ell_t = \log p(t_t \mid t_{<t}, x)$ are recorded as an intrinsic confidence trace over the response.
- **Windows and statistics**: from each trace they extract a handful of candidate windows anchored at the start or end of the response — the first or last $k$ tokens (a fixed count; the paper's features span $k$ of 3, 5, 10, and 30) and the first or last $\alpha T$ tokens (a fraction $\alpha$ of the response length $T$, e.g. the final half) — plus the full response, and summarize each window by its mean, median, min, max, variance, standard deviation, range, and trajectory slope.
- **LLM-as-judge targets**: a separate GPT-5-mini judge reads the debate transcript and scores each argument on five targets, which the confidence statistics are then tested against:
    - *Instruction following* — three-point ordinal (1 = Low, 2 = Medium, 3 = High)
    - *Justification quality* — three-point ordinal
    - *Evidence grounding* — three-point ordinal
    - *Aggregate score* — the composite, in $[0,9]$
    - *Critical failure* — a binary flag for a severe error; when it fires, the aggregate score above is overridden to 0
  Prediction quality is measured per target by its natural metric: Spearman's $\rho$ (and Kendall's $\tau$) for the four ordinal targets, AUROC for the binary critical-failure flag. So "critical-failure detection" is just the binary-classification slice of the analysis — predicting that flag — as opposed to rank-correlating the ordinal scores.

![The multi-agent debate and LLM-as-judge evaluation framework: an Advocate argues an essay's strengths and a Skeptic rebuts, both exposing token-level log-probabilities, which are compared against a judge's rubric scores. Figure 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure1.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure1-full.png"}

## Results

The data is the [ASAP automated-essay-scoring benchmark](https://www.kaggle.com/c/asap-aes) (the Hewlett Foundation's Automated Student Assessment Prize), restricted to Essay Sets 7 and 8 (the only sets with trait-level human annotations). Advocate and Skeptic arguments come from GPT-4o-mini, and the judge is a deterministic GPT-5-mini. Table 1 reports, for each role–target pair, the top three confidence features ranked by their fit to the judge score and the best score achieved.

Early-token confidence is the standout predictor, most clearly for catching severe failures and on the harder essay set:

- **Critical-failure detection is strong.** The max of the first 3 tokens reaches AUROC 0.849 for the Advocate on Set 7, and the median of the first 5 tokens reaches 0.759 on Set 8, so severe errors tend to show up as localized confidence spikes or drops right at the opening.
- **Fine-grained quality ranking is weak.** The best Spearman correlations with ordinal scores top out near 0.39 (Advocate, Set 7), and the Skeptic's barely reach 0.11 to 0.27.
- **Roles are asymmetric.** Confidence aligns with judged quality far better for the supportive Advocate than the adversarial Skeptic, across both sets.
- **Not uniformly early-token.** On Set 7 the Advocate's best ordinal predictor was the full-response median, not an opening-window feature. The early-token advantage shows up mainly on Set 8 and for critical-failure detection.

![Top-3 confidence features for each role–target pair across Essay Sets 7 and 8. For the ordinal targets the final column reports Spearman's $\rho$; for critical-failure detection it reports AUROC. Early-$k$ refers to statistics over the first $k$ generated tokens, final-half to the last 50%. Table 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table1.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="table1-full.png"}

The judge leans hard on its top score — it assigns a 3 to 77% of essays on instruction following, 79% on justification quality, and 93% on evidence grounding. Evidence grounding is so saturated it behaves almost like a constant, which leaves little rank variation for any confidence feature to align with and mechanically holds its correlation down — a ceiling in the labels, not a failure of the signal.

![Distribution of LLM-as-judge scores by dimension: evidence grounding saturates at the top score, while instruction following and justification quality vary more. Figure 3 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure3.png){fig-align="center"}

## My Notes

- **Intrinsic confidence works for open-ended reasoning too.** [Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know](/posts/20260504-kadavath-mostly-know/) established that a model's token probabilities track correctness on closed-form tasks. This paper extends the idea to open-ended, reference-free reasoning and localizes it: the first three to five tokens hold more predictive signal than the full sequence, which makes the proxy a cheap decoding-time read rather than a separate calibration model [[1]](#ref-1).
- **Confidence is diagnostic for advocacy, not for critique.** The Skeptic's log-probability confidence barely correlates with judged quality (Spearman 0.11 to 0.27) while the Advocate's does (up to 0.39, AUROC 0.85). That matches a known soft spot: [MAST](/posts/20250802-mast-multi-agent-failures/) found verification failures — a system not checking its own work — to be a recurring multi-agent breakdown. Here the critique role is also where intrinsic confidence is least informative, so monitoring helps least on the function that most needs a second look.
- **It is a failure flag, not a fine scorer.** Rank agreement with graded quality is weak (Spearman around 0.39 at best), but critical-failure detection is strong (AUROC up to 0.85). And the abstract's "consistently the strongest" is set-dependent: on Essay Set 7 the Advocate's best ordinal predictor was the *full-response median*, not an early-token feature.
- **What can we do with token logits reliably?** Only one thing transfers across the paper's two essay sets: the predictive signal lives in the opening three to five tokens, so early-token statistics make a cheap decode-time screen for severe failures (AUROC up to 0.85 within a set). The specific feature and its direction do not transfer — the top detector is the max of the first three tokens on Set 7 but the median of the first five on Set 8, and the signs even disagree (a confident early spike flags failure, a wide early spread suppresses it). So the reliable recipe is narrow: read the first few tokens, but fit which statistic and which sign on your own data rather than lifting a fixed rule from this paper.

## Related Posts

- [MAST: A Failure Taxonomy for Multi-Agent Systems](/posts/20250802-mast-multi-agent-failures/): the failure-mode map for multi-agent debate that this paper's critical-failure flag tries to catch cheaply from decoding signals.
- [Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know](/posts/20260504-kadavath-mostly-know/): the calibration result this paper extends from closed-form correctness to open-ended, reference-free reasoning quality.
- [Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy](/posts/20260505-semantic-entropy/): another intrinsic, decoding-time uncertainty signal for output quality, against which early-token log-probability is the lighter-weight alternative.
- [SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?](/posts/20260430-selfreflect-internal-distribution/): a counterpoint on whether a model's stated confidence reflects its internal distribution, where this paper reads the distribution directly from log-probabilities instead.
